title: The Cold Hit
protagonist: Dana Osei, forensic statistician, state crime laboratory DNA unit
primary_metric: cold-hit cases closed per detective-and-lab hour

options.A: Refer on Match -- send every cold hit to the DA's office as soon as the database search returns it, no additional lab-side delay
options.B: Hold for Corroboration -- require one independent, non-DNA corroborating check on every cold hit before it is referred

not_found: A specific crime laboratory's annual cold-hit caseload volume -- no state or federal agency publishes this. Became MA1 (60 cases/year).
The share of any lab's annual cold hits that come from a partial (sub-full-panel) profile versus a full profile -- not published anywhere. Became MA2 (60%, twist raises to 100%).
A lab's internal per-case investigative file review time. Became MA3 (6 hours/case).
A specific, published time cost for an independent corroboration step on a DNA cold hit. Became MA4 (3 hours/case).

A published figure for the investigator time cost of walking back a referral that turns out to have been a coincidental match. Became MA5 (200 hours) -- set deliberately well above MA4 to reflect that undoing an already-sent referral (re-investigation, discovery obligations, wrongful-referral exposure) is a materially larger event than the corroboration check would have been.

scenario_constructions: Dana Osei and the specific cold case in this case are fictional, invented for this case -- consistent with corpus convention (e.g. Rosa Delgado / Fermenter, Marcus Feld / The Manifest Split). The state DOJ Bureau of Forensic Services and its data bank program are real (California's, specifically) and cited directly by name and by their real published figures.

The evidence sample recovering exactly 8 of 20 usable loci is a scenario construction, chosen to be realistic for degraded, decade-old evidence per real-world reporting that partial profiles routinely fall short of the full core panel -- not a citation to one specific real case's locus count.

This year's cold-hit caseload (60), its partial-profile share (60%, twist 100%), and the three per-case time costs (6h / 3h / 200h) are constructed to create a genuine, close decision within SPEC Section 2's ~20% balance margin; they are not derived from any single real lab's actual annual operating data.

modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes a specific lab's annual cold-hit volume. Set at a scale consistent with a state DNA unit actively working a backlog, informed by the real published scale of state data-bank hit totals (S1).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Share of this year's cold hits from a partial (sub-20-locus) profile
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes this split for any specific lab. Degraded, older cold-case evidence is realistically more likely to yield a partial profile than fresh evidence.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Base investigative file review time, per case
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes a lab's internal file-review time. Applies equally under both policies.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Corroboration step time, per case (Policy B only)
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes a specific corroboration procedure's time cost. Set as a modest fixed add-on representative of a documented alibi/location cross-check.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Rework cost per false referral (Policy A only)
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes this figure. Set well above the corroboration cost to reflect that walking back an already-sent referral (re-investigation, discovery obligations, wrongful-referral exposure) is materially larger than the corroboration step would have been -- this asymmetry is the basis of the case's tension.

sensitivity_note: SPEC Section 6 applies: this case touches wrongful accusation via a coincidental DNA database match, which is real stakes adjacent to (but not itself) death, illness, or family hardship. Framed as protection (avoiding a wrongful referral) rather than punishment, per SPEC Section 6's protection-over-destruction guidance. Facilitators should flag this for the discussion.

balance.argument_a: Refer on Match wins on this year's actual numbers (10.26% margin) because the expected number of coincidental (false) referrals is still low even for partial-profile hits -- fewer than one expected per year -- so paying a corroboration cost on every single one of this year's 60 cases costs more total hours than absorbing the rare, expensive rework cost only when a false referral actually happens.
balance.argument_b: Hold for Corroboration wins if the caseload shifts toward more degraded, harder-to-resolve evidence -- and a real, disclosed scenario (the twist) shows that threshold is not hypothetical: a grant-funded initiative that specifically clears the most degraded backlog first raises the partial-profile share from 60% to 100%, which is enough to flip the winner, because Policy A's cost scales with the (now higher) expected false-referral count while Policy B's cost per case never changes.
balance.margin_basis: Compute total detective-and-lab hours for each policy from Appendix D/E's caseload and time figures, applying Appendix C's database match probability (via Appendix B's two search-stage sizes) to estimate Policy A's expected false-referral count, then divide the shared caseload count (60, identical under either policy since all cases are eventually closed one way or another) by each policy's total hours.
balance.twist_effect: A grant-funded cold-case initiative specifically targets the most degraded backlog first: instead of 60% of this year's hits being partial-profile, all of them (100%) are. This raises the expected number of coincidental false referrals under Policy A from 0.649/year to 1.081/year, raising Policy A's total hours from 489.75 to 576.24 while Policy B's total (540.0) is unaffected -- the winner flips to Hold for Corroboration, by 6.71%. Disclosed here and in sensitivity_model.py; never in case.md or FACILITATOR.md's student-facing sections.
balance.stability: Base margin (10.26%) is a direct, computable function of all five disclosed Modeling Assumptions (MA1-MA5) via sensitivity_model.py. Per sensitivity_disclosure[], frac_partial, h_corrob, and h_rework each flip the winner or breach the SPEC Section 2 20% cap at a +/-50% flex -- a real, disclosed finding about how tightly this case's margin depends on undisclosed real-world lab-operational data, not a defect introduced by an unscoped sweep. The real cited figures (RMP_locus, N_state, N_national) are deliberately excluded from FLEX -- see sensitivity_model.py's docstring.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA1 has no citable lab-specific source. Flexing +/-50% does NOT change the winner or the margin at all (10.26% both directions) -- n_hits scales every term in both policies' totals proportionally, so it cancels out of the ratio. A facilitator can use this to show why NOT every assumption is equally load-bearing, even when none are cited.

MA2, no citable source. Flexing +50% (to 90%) flips the winner to B (2.71%, within cap); flexing -50% (to 30%) breaches the 20% cap (27.10%, A wins wider). One of the two most load-bearing assumptions -- this is also the exact lever the twist pulls, deliberately, so a facilitator can connect the twist directly back to this disclosure.

MA3, no citable source. Flexing +50% narrows the margin (7.50%, A still wins) without flipping; flexing -50% widens it (16.22%, A still wins, near the cap). Applies equally to both policies, so its effect is real but smaller than the other four.

MA4, no citable source. Flexing +50% breaches the cap (28.64%, A wins wider); flexing -50% flips the winner to B (8.83%, within cap). The single most load-bearing assumption in the model alongside h_rework.

MA5, no citable source. Flexing +50% flips the winner to B (2.71%, within cap); flexing -50% breaches the cap (27.10%, A wins wider). This is the assumption the case's entire tension is built on (the asymmetry between a routine corroboration cost and a rare-but-expensive rework cost) -- unsurprising that it is this load-bearing.

deliverables.text: A random match probability (RMP) calculation for the 8-usable-locus partial profile, using the per-locus match probability and the independent-event multiplication rule.

A two-stage database match probability (DMP) table computing DMP = N x RMP at the state-search stage (no hit) and the national-search stage (hit found), reflecting the real multistage LDIS/SDIS/NDIS search structure.
A cases-closed-per-detective-hour comparison for Policy A vs. Policy B using this year's caseload and per-case time costs, with the percent margin between them.

A combination-vs-permutation calculation: the number of 10-locus subsets of CODIS's 20-locus panel (combination) versus the number of ordered 10-of-20 selections (permutation), with a written explanation of why locus-subset choice is a combination problem.

A written explanation, using Population, Sample, and Convenience Sampling, of why the searched offender database is not a random sample of the general population and what that means for interpreting a cold hit.
